summary: Learning space mission design is typically limited to abstract theory. Students and aspiring engineers study orbital mechanics, spacecraft design, or rocket launches in isolation, lacking an interactive environment to experiment with an entire mission. To address this challenge our solution is "Blackout Space Mission". It is a free, browser-based 3D game where students aged design a satellite, launch it, and simulate a real space mission. The most important part: a game allows participants to experiment, make decisions, encounter constraints, and learn I from both successful and unsuccessful missions. Potential approaches include mission planning, spacecraft configuration, instrument selection, resource management, orbital selection, launch planning, communications, and mission simulation. Using authentic NASA planetary data, the game models complex engineering trade-offs, showing how every component choice affects mass, budget, energy, and mission survival. Instead of a simple pass or fail, every launch triggers a detailed simulation review. If a mission fails, our onboard Al assistant Orbi explains the exact physics and engineering reasons behind it, such as running out of battery during prolonged eclipses in low orbit. So our project brings educational value too. Players are then given constructive hints and a chance to redesign, turning every failure into a valuable learning experience. Our game is available for every person with every level of knowledge in science.
details:
Blackout Space Mission is a free, browser-based 3D simulation game where all people can design a satellite, launch it, and simulate a real space mission.

Players follow a structured four-step workflow:

First, choosing a mission goal (such as studying Mars' atmosphere, imaging Earth, monitoring disasters, or mapping the Moon);

Second, assembling a spacecraft in a hangar from real components: Body, Panels, Batteries, Computer, Pointing, Antennas, Instruments, Engine, Cooling). Player can design their satellite on its own and change it , paint it.

Third, selecting an optimal orbit and rocket; Our mission especially depends on these factors.

Users in our game should choose components wisely and think properly before adding them to our mission because must be taken into account the main things like: Budget, Mass, Power, Fuel.

Fourth, running a physics-based launch simulation. It allows a player an proper observation of its own mission and confirmation of project success.

Instead of a simple pass-or-fail screen, the game provides meaningful feedback: if a mission fails, the onboard Al assistant Orbi clearly explains the physics, mistakes and engineering root causes (such as battery drain during long eclipses in low orbit), and gives a chance to improve and remake mission, turning failures into powerful learning moments. If there is a success, We can travel to the planet that was constructed by help of NASA official dataset. Overall, our project transforms abstract, isolated aerospace theory into an engaging, interactive engineering playground and have lots of benefits and novelty.

OUR impact of the project:

Built using a modular C# object-oriented architecture (PlanetInfo, RocketDef, Part, Build).

Cross-references component specifications with authentic NASA planetary datasets to calculate real-time aerospace physics and system-wide constraints.

Platform: Browser-based 3D environment featuring an interactive Ul, virtual hangar workspace, and an Al assistant dialogue system.

How is our project creative?

It uniquely combines a 3D building experience with an interactive Al mentor (Orbi) that guides players through design flaws and conducts physics-based post-mortem failure analysis. It is not only about making a satellit, it also provides learning new things and technologies. It offers dual modes-a structured, goal-oriented Mission campaign with leaderboards and a free-form Sandbox mode for creative exploration.

What factors did your team consider?

Target Audience Suitability: Designed specifically for students but also for different aged people ensuring that omplex aerospace physics are approachable, intuitive, and educational rather than overwhelming.

Real-World Fidelity vs. Playability: Balanced authentic engineering constraints (mass, budget, thermal limits, and power management) with engaging gameplay loops, teamwork features (supporting up to 4 players), and clear visual progress across the four distinct game stages.

Built for a Global Audience&Language: With seamless language switching and a free, browser-based format,

"Blackout" is accessible to students anywhere in the world, breaking down language barriers in STEM education and letting future explorers learn in the language they know best.
